claim: `ALTER TABLE … MOVE PART|PARTITION TO DISK/VOLUME 'ca'` and background TTL/policy moves must copy a part to a content-addressed disk as one atomic unit: one part, one manifest, one ref, published atomically with deduplication.

The MOVE-to-CA implementation has two independent defects: the part-path parser routes files under `<table>/moving/<part>/` to the literal ref `moving`, and `DataPartStorageOnDiskBase::clonePart` copies files through separate autocommit transactions that a CA disk cannot use for a multi-file part.
On the Atomic layout, `moving` already occupies the parser's part-directory position, so the L1 fix adds a `route()` case rather than changing `findPartDirComponent` for that layout.
`ContentAddressed::kMovingDirName` is the reserved constant whose value is `moving` for MOVE staging paths.
For an Atomic path `uui/uuid-1/moving/all_1_1_0/data.bin`, `parsePartFilePath` reports `table_uuid=uuid-1`, `part_name=moving`, and `file=all_1_1_0/data.bin`.

The plan's Atomic-layout `route()` contract folds `moving/<part>/<file>` into the live table namespace with ref `<part>` and file `<file>`, while a bare `<table>/moving` container has an empty ref and file.

On non-Atomic tables, `data/<db>/<table>/moving/<part>/<file>` needs an explicit `moving` anchor because the right-to-left part-directory scan otherwise anchors on the inner part and creates the spurious table id `data/<db>/<table>/moving`.
The non-Atomic parser must treat both `detached` and `moving` as reserved table-level directories and anchor on the first such component after the table prefix.

The generic `clonePart` path uses `copyDirectoryContent` and `IDisk::copyFile` to create a fresh autocommit transaction per file, and a later content file raises `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` with `Autocommit writes are not supported for content part files`.
`freeze` cannot provide the MOVE-to-CA copy primitive because its transactional `Backup()` path uses same-disk `transaction->copyFile`, which throws `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` for cross-disk CA copies.

The CA branch of `DataPartStorageOnDiskBase::clonePart` creates one destination transaction, recursively streams every source file through non-autocommit `IDiskTransaction::writeFile`, and commits once.
Cross-disk CA part copying is sequential because the transaction's staging map is not mutex-guarded and MOVE is latency-insensitive; parallel copying is deferred optimization work.
The CA-specific `clonePart` branch is gated by `dst_disk->isContentAddressed()`, while non-CA destinations retain the existing directory-copy path.
If a CA clone fails, its self-created transaction is undone and the exception is rethrown; a successful clone is then opened with `create(..., initialize=true)`.
The MOVE-to-CA smoke contract is that `disk_name` changes `default → ca_smoke → default`, row checksums remain identical, and neither `Code: 236` nor a `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` exception occurs.
The S36 dedup-on-TO-CA check uses deterministic `repeat('cas-move-dedup-probe-', 100)` payloads so a second move of byte-identical content must observe `CasBlobPutDedup > 0` and `CasBlobPut == 0`.

Same-pool `CA↔CA` moves are deferred for verification rather than special-cased; `CA→local` moves and insert-time policy routing are explicitly out of scope because they already work through a plain `DiskLocal` destination.

Scenario S36 found that TO-CA MOVE was unimplemented: the generic mover copied files independently, producing `Code 236 promote: ref 'moving' already names a different committed manifest` or `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` for a column file.
Without a `MOVING_DIR_NAME` parser case, every file under `<table>/moving/<part>/` routes to the literal ref `moving`, causing all files and all moved parts to collide.

TO-CA MOVE must preserve deduplication, concurrent SELECT availability, clean `fsck`, bounded GC reclamation of the vacated side, and restart atomicity such that a part is fully moved or remains fully on its origin.

The `freeze` transaction seam cannot be reused for cross-disk MOVE because `DiskObjectStorageTransaction::copyFile` calls `generateObjectKeyForPath`, which throws `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` on CA, while generic disk copy primitives use autocommit writes.
The corrected identity design publishes a cloned part under transient ref `moving/<part>` and makes `rename(moving/<part> → <part>)` a committed-ref repoint onto the final ref.

Publishing directly under final ref `<part>` is rejected because a failure between clone commit and swap would leak an unreclaimed final ref and collide with the generic rename destination precheck; the `moving/<part>` prefix lets startup cleanup reclaim the transient ref.

Deferring `clonePart`'s commit into the swap is rejected because `clonePart` must commit before `create(initialize=true)` reads the part back, and changing that contract would enlarge the generic mover surface.

The L2 fix copies every part file sequentially through one destination CA transaction and commits once, causing `publishStaging` and `PartWriteTxn` to upload deduplicated blobs, create one manifest, and publish one ref atomically.
Both L1 identity routing and L2 whole-part atomicity are required: L2 alone still collides on ref `moving`, while L1 alone still autocommits per file and can raise `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`.
`MOVE PARTITION` clones each part independently through `moveParts`, so one-part-per-transaction is the correct granularity; `CA→local` remains untouched.

Same-pool `CA↔CA` movement is deferred because the target should deduplicate existing pool content, but it remains unverified whether the target final ref `<part>` collides with the source ref `<part>`.

The MOVE test gate includes `MOVE PART` and `MOVE PARTITION` in both directions, concurrent SELECTs, `fsck` with `dangling=0`, bounded GC reclamation, restart complete-or-rollback behavior, and dedup-on-TO-CA.
The `MOVING_DIR_NAME` unit case must map `moving/<part>/<file>` to `(live namespace, <part>, <file>)`.

`RefTableState::committed` is replaced by an ordered COW map so copies in `CasRefLedger::flushRefBatch` and `applyRefLogTxn`/`admits` cost O(touched rows), while behavior, snapshot bytes, admission decisions, and errors remain byte-identical.

`RefCowMap` consists of an immutable shared `std::shared_ptr<const std::map<String, RefCommittedRow>> base` and a per-copy `std::map<String, std::optional<RefCommittedRow>> overlay`, with present entries as overrides and `nullopt` as tombstones.

`RefCowMap` copies share the immutable base and copy only the overlay, keyed reads check overlay before base, point writes modify overlay, ordered iteration merges both sorted ranges, and `materialize()` folds the overlay into a fresh base once per flush.

The planned `RefCowMap` API is a read-only-iterator, `std::map<String, RefCommittedRow>`-compatible subset covering keyed lookup, ordered iteration, size/empty, emplace, insert-or-assign, erase, equality, and materialization.
`RefCowMap::size()` and `empty()` are O(1) because `net_delta` tracks overlay inserts and tombstones relative to the immutable base size.
`RefCowMap::materialize()` merges overlay values and tombstones into a new immutable base, then clears the overlay and resets `net_delta`.
`RefCowMap` has no mutable-reference iterator: a row update must copy the found `RefCommittedRow`, modify it, and write it back with `insert_or_assign`.

The COW map's randomized property test must compare insert, update, erase, find, size, ordered iteration, and materialize operations against `std::map<String, RefCommittedRow>`, including copy-then-mutate isolation.

Changing `RefTableState::committed` to `RefCowMap` leaves keyed-read and ordered-iteration consumers compatible; `CasRefProtocol.cpp::applySetPayload` is the exceptional site that must be rewritten for read-only iterators.
`RefCowMap` preserves canonical snapshot ordering by bytewise `ref_name`, so the codec boundary remains `std::vector<RefCommittedRow>` and snapshot bytes remain unchanged.
The COW map is scoped to `RefTableState::committed`; `precommits` remains `std::set`, the base remains `std::map` in this cut, and no other state field changes.

`CasRefLedger::flushRefBatch` must call `rt->state.committed.materialize()` immediately after installing `final_txn` under the existing `state_mutex`, so later trial copies stay proportional to the current flush.
Without install-time materialization, the COW overlay grows across successful flushes and later `working = rt->state` copies regress toward copying all rows touched over the object's lifetime.

The persistent ordered-tree approach, an `absl::btree_map` base, and changes to `precommits` are out of scope for the COW-map cut; commit-path tracing and microbenchmark evidence are separate follow-up work.
The ref-table COW change is scoped to `RefTableState::committed` and is intended to be pure performance work with byte-identical behavior.
The commit-heavy ref-table workload's dominant copy cost is deep-copying `std::map<String, RefCommittedRow>`, while a typical batch item touches about one ref.
Hot ref-table paths are keyed lookups, while `snapshotOf`, `listRefs`, and `dropNamespace` are the cold paths that require full scans.
Ordered iteration is load-bearing because `snapshotOf` and removal-transaction construction require bytewise-sorted iteration by `ref_name`; an unordered overlay is insufficient.

The ref-table isolation invariant remains that leaders copy state under `state_mutex`, validate and PUT without the lock, and reacquire the lock only to install the result, while readers hold the lock for their entire in-place read.
The COW overlay uses a sorted `std::map` because ordered merge iteration is required; a persistent immutable ordered tree is deferred because no drop-in implementation exists in the tree.
`RefCowMap` keyed access checks overlay entries first, treats tombstones as misses, writes only to overlay, and performs sorted two-range merge iteration for cold full scans.
`RefCowMap::materialize()` is O(n) once per flush and restores `base + empty overlay`, so ordinary keyed reads between flushes access the base without merge overhead.
Sharing `std::shared_ptr<const map>` introduces no new locking: trial copies retain private overlays, installation swaps state under `state_mutex`, and detached snapshots encode outside the lock.
Only `RefTableState::committed` changes; the codec remains based on `std::vector<RefCommittedRow>`, and the base container stays `std::map` with an optional future `absl::btree_map` follow-up.

The COW implementation must pass equivalence tests against `std::map`, an O(1)-copy assertion, byte-identical `snapshotOf` output, the existing `Ca*:Cas*` battery, and a trace check that `__copy_construct_tree` is no longer a top ref-table stack.
A persistent immutable ordered tree is deferred, `absl::btree_map` is optional follow-up work, and `precommits` remains unchanged.

Review finding №1 is a partial real fix: conditional S3 copy can fall back to unconditional copying, but the common single-operation path is probe-guarded and the remaining gap is multipart copies larger than 32 MiB.

Review finding №2 is by design at the harm level: unconditional `resurrectStaged` is safe because content-addressed payloads are byte-identical, promote dependencies are tokenless-on-ref, and fresh tags defeat stale exact-token deletes.
Review finding №3 is refuted because `HEAD` precedes `GET`; a mixed result can contain newer bytes with an older token, and conditional consumers fail closed on that stale-token combination.
Review finding №4 is real: if `writeCondemnedMeta` is swallowed, a writer can adopt the retired token and a later exact-token GC delete can remove a blob still referenced by a committed edge.

Review finding №5 is real: pre-CAS generation pruning based only on the proposed seal can delete a run still referenced by a winning concurrent leader's parent seal, permanently wedging GC with `CORRUPTED_DATA` in `PriorEdgeCursor`.

Review finding №6 is real: a sender can release its source part while a receiver's `precommitAdd` edge PUT is stalled across at least two GC folds, allowing the only same-token blob reference to be reclaimed.

Review finding №7 is real: the receiver compares the advertised pool only on the sender, so a reservation can select a non-CA disk or a different CA pool and publish a dangling manifest or throw before byte fallback.
Review finding №8 includes a confirmed scheduler UAF: `runGarbageCollectionRoundNow` snapshots `gc_scheduler.get()` under a mutex, unlocks, and can dereference it after shutdown resets the scheduler.
Review finding №9 is real: decommission can delete a successor's fresh mount and epoch objects after releasing the impersonated lease, violating durable epoch monotonicity.

Review finding №10 is a real TSan data race on the plain `std::function` event sink because `setEventSink` runs after `Pool::open` starts the renewal thread, although the traced timing refutes crash-grade overlap.
Review finding №11 is a narrow metadata leak: a build allocated before registration can outlive namespace drop and GC reclamation, then create a reborn Live-but-ownerless empty ref table.

Review finding №12's call-time mutation of durable refs is by design: `renameParts` is the commit point and rollback compensates with new operations over committed disk state, but `removeDirectory` must discard staged entries when removing a part before commit.

Review finding №13 is real hardening: telemetry emitted after durable ref publication must not turn a successful operation into a caller-visible failure; post-durable emission should catch, log, and continue.

Review finding №14 leaves the `CityHash128` default as a design decision: `sha256` is available for hostile shared-pool threat models, while same-trust-domain replicas retain the default under the current model.

Review finding №15 leaves shared local-pool startup behavior as a design decision because single-server ownership cannot be proved inside the process, and changing INFO to WARNING would break default CA-over-local tests.

Review finding №16 is real: `ReadPipeline::tryBuildReaderExecutor` does not fall back for `file_view`, so a CA read can expose the `CHCA` envelope header and shift offsets when `use_reader_executor=1` and `remote_filesystem_read_method='read'`.
Review finding №17 leaves unknown GCS bucket versioning as an explicit-WARNING tradeoff: confirmed `Enabled` fails, but an unverifiable check proceeds to avoid overly aggressive mount refusal.

Review finding №18 is real: emulated `get`/`head` tokens use `TokenType::Emulated` while list tokens use `TokenType::ETag`, so listed-token conditional deletes fail safely but generation-prune accounting can report deletion while objects leak.
Review finding №19 is a low-harm but real wire-contract issue: conditional mutations send only `Token.value`, so callers should reject mismatched token types before any conditional operation.

Review finding №19c is latent local-CA data loss across restart: a non-persisted `emu_seq` can re-mint a persisted condemn token value, allowing `deleteExact` to delete a live incarnation after restart.

Review finding №20 is split: decoder identity fields need hygiene checks, duplicate JSON keys already throw `CORRUPTED_DATA`, and fold seals lack a key-to-generation binding that could corrupt the GC cursor or cause premature deletion.
Review finding №21 is real: casting a decoded `uint64` version to `uint32` before validation turns `4294967299` into version `3` and can bypass compatibility checks.
Review finding №22 is real: `gc_interval_sec=0` causes back-to-back GC rounds, while `gc_shards=0` makes `gc/state` unreadable and can trigger modulo-by-zero, permanently wedging GC.
Review finding №23 is real: CA `truncateFile` silently succeeds without changing bytes, so it should raise `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` because immutable blobs require whole-file replacement.
Review finding №24 is real: `unlinkFile` ignores `if_exists`, so removing a nonexistent file can silently succeed instead of raising `FILE_DOESNT_EXIST` for the non-`if_exists` API.

Review finding №25 is latent terminal-transaction hardening: a failed `commit` can leave `PartStaging::published=true`, causing a hypothetical retry on the same transaction object to skip work and report success.
Review finding №26 is a real stale-payload mechanism but deferred because the only production appender is the single-writer, per-mutation-unique `MergeTreeMutationEntry::writeCSN` path.
Review finding №27 is by design: `source absent && destination present → success` makes single-writer, deterministically-derived renames idempotent under re-drive.
Review finding №28 is real: `Pool::beginPartWrite` can register a build sequence before construction fails, permanently pinning the GC `minActive` retention floor until remount.
Review finding №29 leaves an experimental gate for `metadata_type=content_addressed` as upstream/release work, while the fork's soak and CI lanes intentionally remain ungated.

Review finding №30 is real for started disks: `system.content_addressed_mounts` skips listing exceptions and can make a failed listing appear as no mounts, although not-started disks are legitimately skipped.

Review finding №31 is real: an explicit `staging_backend=s3` can silently fall back to local staging after a failed conditional-copy probe, unexpectedly consuming local disk and hiding a configuration mismatch.

The CAS GC graduation rule must require confirmed durable `Condemned` metadata for the exact `(hash, token)`; absent confirmation carries the entry to the next round instead of deleting, without changing the rule that a 404 during fold must not throw.
Pre-CAS generation pruning must protect the union of generations referenced by both the proposed seal and the parent seal; only generations referenced by neither may be deleted before the CAS.

Relink handoff retention requires a sender-created build-owned epoch-floor pin that remains until the receiver's edge is durable; otherwise a same-token blob can be reclaimed during a stalled handoff.
A receiver must compare the reservation-selected disk's CA pool UUID with the advertised pool UUID and use byte fallback for either a non-CA disk or a different pool.

The emulated backend should derive `TokenType::Emulated` token values from the underlying local-object etag so list and head agree and a post-restart fresh incarnation cannot match a persisted exact-token delete.
The GC configuration factory must reject `gc_interval_sec=0` and `gc_shards=0` before pool open, and `encodeGcState` must raise a runtime exception rather than rely on a release-inert `chassert`.
Decommission must inspect every `DeleteOutcome`, abort the tail on any non-`Deleted` result, and delete mount before the claimed epoch and owner so successor objects cannot be reclaimed.
The triage fix wave applies confirmed real fixes with fail-closed behavior, while deferring the six user design decisions №14, №15, №17, №29, №30, and №31.

GC keeps its asynchronous advisory metadata model, but graduation to `delete_pending` or redelete requires confirmed durable `Condemned` metadata for the exact `(hash, token)`; missing evidence causes a fail-safe carry.
The planned GC marker confirmation can come from a successful marker write in the current or earlier round or from a fresh `loadMeta(hash)` observing `state == Condemned && token == entry.token`.

Emulated object tokens must use the underlying object's etag value with `TokenType::Emulated`, and conditional operations must reject an expected token whose type differs from the backend's minting type.
Pre-CAS generation pruning must include every generation referenced by the parent seal as well as the proposed seal, because a losing leader must not delete a run referenced by the winning leader.
`gc_interval_sec` and `gc_shards` must both be at least 1; zero values must fail with `BAD_ARGUMENTS` before opening a content-addressed pool.
The decommission tail must delete the farewell mount token first, then the epoch token captured under the claim, and owner last; every non-`Deleted` result aborts the tail and retains the slot.
After fetch reservation, a relink is allowed only when the chosen disk is CA and its pool UUID equals the advertised pool UUID; otherwise the code must invoke the existing byte-fetch fallback.
`ReadPipeline::tryBuildReaderExecutor` must include `file_view` in its fallback condition until the executor supports CA payload windows.
When `if_none_match` is present, both S3 copy fallback branches must rethrow the original error rather than degrade to an unconditional read/write copy.
The CAS scheduler lifecycle fix must hold `gc_scheduler_mutex` across `runOneRoundNow`, reject lazy creation after shutdown, and synchronize `cas_store` and `part_access` reads with shutdown resets.
The CAS event sink must be installed in `PoolConfig` or `Pool::open` before `mountWritable` starts the renewal thread; `setEventSink` is retained only as a pre-open test hook.
CA `truncateFile` must throw `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` because blobs are immutable and whole-file rewrites replace the staged entry.
CA `unlinkFile` must raise `FILE_DOESNT_EXIST` for a missing committed path when `if_exists` is false and be a no-op when `if_exists` is true.
A content-addressed transaction that fails `commit` is terminal: later `commit` or `tryCommit` must throw `LOGICAL_ERROR` instead of retrying the failed object.
The triage backlog defers the fetch-handoff pin for №6, a GC backstop for empty ownerless Live namespaces for №11, and `casAppendObject` for №26 until a concurrent appender is introduced.

CAS blob freshness-meta writes on the INSERT/merge hot path bypass the budgeted `CasRequestController`: `putMetaIfAbsent`, `casMeta`, and `deleteMetaExact` call backend conditional operations directly.

The S22 fix must route blob-meta conditional writes through a controller that resolves ambiguous attempts by token and byte checks, and must propagate exhaustion rather than swallow a metadata write failure.
The S40 data-loss gate is `lost == 0` for every server-acked insert, while cross-replica dedup-line counts are observation-only because legitimate client-timeout-then-commit retries also deduplicate.
A failed S40 fault schedule or zero outage-induced insert failures makes the run vacuous and must fail its anti-vacuity verdict instead of passing silently.
The deterministic `build/dl_probe.py` reproduction submitted and acknowledged 1314 inserts, found 1116 present, and lost 198 acknowledged rows during a 105-second RustFS pause and replica kill.

The smoking-gun log says `Block with ID all_10341432382904313846_13999145979494917125 already exists on other replicas as part all_1117_1117_0; ignoring it.`, while `all_1117_1117_0` was absent from both replicas.

During the outage, Keeper committed the `block_id` znode and part-znode `all_1117_1117_0` even though the CA blobs and manifest did not durably reach paused RustFS and the committing replica was then killed.
R3's `NETWORK_ERROR` with `retry-later` caused a byte-identical retry to reuse the same `block_id`; cross-replica dedup found the phantom znode and returned success without inserting rows.
The CA integrity oracle can remain clean during this loss because no dangling CAS ref exists; only a row-count or checksum oracle detects the missing acknowledged rows.

`39cf3279652` removed CA publish-at-rename and moved publication into `ContentAddressedTransaction::commit`, creating the CA split-commit window; R3 changed the resulting ambiguity into a client-visible retry that amplified silent loss.
For `all_1117_1117_0`, `system.part_log` recorded only `RemovePart`, and the fault-window blob log recorded 112 failed uploads, confirming that the phantom's CAS data never durably landed.

The refined root cause is that the `block_id` and part-znode survive removal of a part whose CA blob PUTs failed, so the surviving block-id znode outlives CAS-blob durability and falsely deduplicates a byte-identical retry.
The report's earlier claim that `renameParts` performed the CA publish before the Keeper multi is explicitly corrected as false; on CA `renameParts` is only a tmp-to-final overlay re-key.

In the failing interleaving, `ReplicatedMergeTreeSink::commitPart` builds Keeper ops, calls `transaction.renameParts()`, executes `tryMultiNoThrow(ops)` to commit block-id and part-znode, and only then calls `transaction.commit()` to upload blobs and publish the CA ref.
When RustFS is paused, `uploadPendingBlobs` in the post-Keeper `ContentAddressedTransaction::commit` hangs until the CAS budget and throws; the transaction destructor then rolls back the local part.
After the first attempt, Keeper contains the block-id and part-znode while no replica contains part data, creating a phantom part.

On the retry, `getActiveContainingPart` returns null, so the existing block-id is treated as cross-replica dedup and the server emits `INSERT_WAS_DEDUPLICATED` with HTTP 200 despite inserting no rows.

The required invariant is that a part is durable on its disk before its `block_id` and part-znode are registered in Keeper; parts-transaction commit only flips visibility, while rollback compensates with new operations over committed disk state.

The old `ReplicatedMergeTreeSink::commitPart` order was `renameParts` → Keeper multi → `transaction.commit`, with part disk transactions committed only inside `transaction.commit` after the Keeper decision and under the `data_parts` lock.

Local disks are durable at `renameParts`, plain upstream S3 defers local metadata including tmp-to-final rename until disk commit, and post-`39cf3279652` CA deferred blobs, manifest, and ref publication until disk commit.
A surviving `block_id` has an independent rolling `replicated_deduplication_window`, so a byte-identical retry can be acknowledged as deduplicated after the phantom part-znode is cleaned.
The generic fix closes every part disk-storage transaction in `MergeTreeData::Transaction::renameParts` after deferred renames, with no CA-specific code change.
After `renameParts` returns, every part is durable at its final name; `Transaction::commit` only changes in-memory visibility, and rollback removes or compensates committed disk data.

The `hasActiveTransaction` guard is required because `commitTransaction` resets the storage transaction pointer and calling it on a closed transaction raises `LOGICAL_ERROR`; repeated `renameParts` is therefore idempotent.
With the durability fix, a disk publish failure throws from `renameParts` before the Keeper multi, so no block-id znode exists and a retry inserts honestly.
A crash between the Keeper multi and the later parts-transaction commit leaves the part durable at its final name, with a CA ref in the pool, so restart can see the part.

If a later failure occurs after `renameParts`, rollback removes all preactive parts; published CA parts are reclaimed by ref removal and unpublished parts by temporary cleanup and destructor abandon, before any Keeper multi is reached.

All audited `renameParts` call sites execute before an external commit decision or immediately before `commit` with no intervening decision, and paths bypassing it were found not to violate the durability invariant.

Moving CA disk commit from `Transaction::commit` to `renameParts` moves S3 publish I/O off the `data_parts` lock without changing total I/O volume; the accepted cost is redo work when a later external decision rejects the part.

Verify-on-dedup remains out of scope as the primary fix because it adds a read to every dedup hit and does not close merge-path ordering windows; CA-only publish-at-rename and a new `IDiskTransaction::precommit` phase were also rejected.

The targeted regression failpoint is `part_storage_fail_commit_transaction` in `DataPartStorageOnDiskFull::commitTransaction`; the generic `disk_object_storage_fail_commit_metadata_transaction` is unsuitable because it also fires on autocommit temporary-directory operations.

The failpoint regression test must make the first deduplicated INSERT fail before Keeper registration, retry the identical row after disabling the failpoint, and observe `count() = 1` rather than the pre-fix false-dedup result `0`.

The implementation closes each active part transaction in `renameParts` after deferred `renameTo`, while borrowed projection sub-parts do not independently commit because they share the parent's transaction.

The permanent S40 gate requires a real outage schedule, at least one outage-induced insert exception, a meaningful acknowledged volume, and zero acknowledged-but-absent rows; dedup log counts are non-gating observations.
The structural defect is that `MergeTreeData::Transaction` treats disk durability as a nested side effect of its commit, while rollback never calls an undo or abort operation on the disk transaction.

The intended protocol is prepare durable and compensable storage before the Keeper decision, then apply visibility with a cheap finalize or compensate on abort; `renameParts` is the existing lock-free prepare slot.

The agreed fix model closes the disk transaction at `renameParts`; a later parts-transaction commit has nothing left to do on disk, while rollback performs compensation as a new operation over committed state.

Upstream plain S3 also violates part-before-Keeper durability on a process crash because blob data streams during write but local metadata, including tmp-to-final rename, remains queued until after the Keeper multi.

`rename_in_transaction` controls the lock scope of part materialization, not durability: true defers rename to off-lock `renameParts`, while false performs immediate rename for plain-engine race protection.

A `renameParts` failure occurs after parts are already `PreActive`, so rollback removes the in-memory parts and their disk data; a partial multi-part publish is covered by the same rollback, and no Keeper multi is reached.
Fix commit `77484196b0d` landed the generic `renameParts` transaction close, and the validation reported S40 10/10, `dl_probe` LOST=0, S39 dev 11/11, S36 26/26, and a clean 20-minute seed-42 soak.
The narrower hazard in which a block-id outlives a durably committed part that is lost later remains a separate pre-existing concern; verify-on-dedup is the candidate mitigation.
The stabilization campaign rule is that there are no tolerated known reds; tactical tolerance requires a tracked return item, and standing exceptions require a complete RCA approved by the user.
